name: The Fool
symbolism: A young figure in colourful clothes stands at the edge of a cliff with face turned to the sky, as if not noticing the drop. In one hand the figure holds a white rose, over one shoulder carries a staff with a small bundle, and a little white dog leaps at their feet. Behind them a bright sun shines and snowy peaks can be seen.
upright: The Fool invites you to look at the situation with fresh eyes, without the weight of earlier assumptions. This is the energy of the first step, with more curiosity in it than plan. The card may suggest that it is worth giving yourself the right not to know and to learn along the way. The dog at the Fool's feet is a reminder that openness goes well with a little attentiveness.
reversed: The reversed Fool may point to hesitation before setting out or, on the contrary, to a haste that overlooks important signals. Sometimes it is an invitation to check whether the fear of making a mistake is taking away the joy of trying.
reflection: What would be possible if you did not have to know the ending in advance?
Which small step into the unknown tempts you right now?
advice: This is a good moment for a new beginning. Take the first step even if you do not know the whole way: trust your intuition and curiosity, just watch where you put your feet.
adviceReversed: Pause for a moment before you leap. Check whether the hesitation comes from good sense or from fear of making a mistake, and only then set off.

name: The Magician
symbolism: A figure in a white robe and red cloak raises a wand to the sky with one hand and points to the earth with the other. Above their head is the sign of infinity, and on the table lie a cup, a sword, a pentacle and a wand: the signs of the four elements. The whole scene is framed by blooming roses and lilies.
upright: The Magician speaks of a moment when you have more resources to hand than it seems. The card encourages you to join thought with action and give your intentions a concrete shape. It is a good moment to notice your own talents and use them consciously. The gesture pointing both up and down is a reminder to join vision with everyday practice.
reversed: Reversed, the Magician's energy can scatter: there are plenty of ideas but no direction. It can also be a signal to look at whether your words and intentions are consistent with each other.
reflection: Which skills do you already have at your disposal, though you rarely notice them?
Which thought is waiting to be turned into a first concrete move?
advice: You have everything you need to begin. Take matters into your own hands, focus on one goal and act.
adviceReversed: Before you act, check your intentions. Scattered energy or an attempt to manipulate the situation will not bring you what you want.

name: The High Priestess
symbolism: A woman in blue robes sits between two pillars, one dark and one light, marked with the letters B and J. On her lap she holds a partly hidden scroll, a crescent moon lies at her feet, and behind her hangs a veil decorated with pomegranates. On her head she wears a crown that recalls the phases of the Moon.
upright: The High Priestess invites you to listen to what is quiet and unspoken. Not all answers come through analysis; some ripen in stillness. The card may suggest that it is worth pausing before a decision and giving yourself time to feel the situation. It is a space for trusting your own sense of things.
reversed: The reversed High Priestess may point to intuition being drowned out by the noise of everyday life or by other people's opinions. Sometimes it also means withdrawing too far into yourself when a conversation could bring relief.
reflection: What does your inner voice tell you when you quieten your surroundings for a moment?
What do you need more time for before you make a decision?
advice: The answer is already in you. Do not decide in a hurry: grow quiet and listen to your intuition before you ask others.
adviceReversed: Stop drowning out your inner voice with other people's opinions. Give yourself a moment of quiet and you will see what you really feel.

name: The Empress
symbolism: A woman in a dress patterned with pomegranates rests on soft cushions among ripening wheat. On her head is a wreath of twelve stars, and beside her stands a heart-shaped shield bearing the sign of Venus. In the background a stream flows and a dense forest rustles.
upright: The Empress is a reminder of what grows when it receives attention and tenderness: projects, relationships, and care for yourself too. The card encourages you to appreciate the pleasure of simple things. It may be an invitation to create without the pressure of perfection. This is an energy of generosity that includes you as well.
reversed: Reversed, this energy can show as giving beyond your strength or overlooking your own needs. It can also signal a creative block, which is eased by rest rather than pressure.
reflection: What in your life needs patient care right now in order to grow?
How can you look after yourself today the way you look after others?
advice: Look after what you want to grow: yourself, a relationship, an idea. Act with care and patience, and the matter will take shape of its own accord.
adviceReversed: It is hard to give to others when your own strength is running low. Start by looking after yourself, then care for the rest.

name: The Emperor
symbolism: A bearded ruler in armour and a red cloak sits on a stone throne decorated with rams' heads. In one hand he holds a sceptre topped with an ankh, in the other a golden orb. Behind him rise stark, rust-coloured mountains.
upright: The Emperor speaks of an order that gives a sense of security and lets you act calmly. The card may encourage you to set clear rules, boundaries or a plan. It is also an invitation to take responsibility for your own area of influence. A good structure need not be rigid; it can be a support.
reversed: The reversed Emperor may point to too much control or, on the contrary, to a lack of fixed points of support. It is worth asking whether the present rules still serve you or only restrict you.
reflection: Which boundary or rule would help you feel more secure?
Where does control give you support, and where does it begin to limit you?
advice: Bring in order. Set clear rules, make a plan and take responsibility for the decision: stability will give you the advantage.
adviceReversed: Too much control can stifle the situation. Loosen rigid rules or, if structure is missing, finally build it.

name: The Hierophant
symbolism: A priest in a red robe and a triple crown sits between two stone pillars, raising his hand in blessing. Crossed keys lie at his feet, and before him kneel two disciples in robes decorated with roses and lilies.
upright: The Hierophant refers to knowledge passed down from generation to generation and to communities that give a sense of belonging. The card may suggest drawing on the experience of a teacher, a mentor or a proven method. It is also an opportunity to consider which values are truly your own. Tradition can be a bridge, not a wall.
reversed: The reversed Hierophant may invite you to question rules accepted without thinking. Sometimes it points to a need to find your own way beyond well-worn patterns.
reflection: From whom could you learn something right now?
Which beliefs taken over from others are worth rethinking today?
advice: Use a path that has proved itself. Ask someone experienced for advice, or rely on principles that have already worked.
adviceReversed: You do not have to do everything the way it “should” be done. Ask yourself which rules are yours and which are merely inherited.

name: The Lovers
symbolism: A naked woman and man stand in a garden, and above them, in the clouds, hovers a winged angel with outstretched arms. Behind the woman grows a fruit tree with a serpent coiled around it, behind the man a tree with flame-like leaves. Between them, in the distance, rises a lone mountain.
upright: The Lovers speak of closeness, but also of choices that come from what matters to us. The card may concern a relationship in which honesty and reciprocity count. It may also invite a decision in line with your own values, even if it takes courage. Harmony between heart and action gives a sense of inner order.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to a gap between what you desire and what you choose. It can also be an invitation to an honest conversation about expectations in a relationship.
reflection: Which choice would be most in line with what you truly value?
What do you need in order to feel fully yourself in a relationship?
advice: You face a choice. Choose in line with your values, not with convenience. Go for what truly matters to you.
adviceReversed: Something does not add up: the heart wants one thing and your actions say another. Before you decide, honestly name what you want.

name: The Chariot
symbolism: A warrior in armour decorated with crescent moons stands in a stone chariot under a canopy strewn with stars. The chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, one black and one white, looking in different directions. Behind him are the walls of a city and a flowing river.
upright: The Chariot describes the energy of focused movement, in which different forces are steered in one direction. The card may encourage perseverance and a clear statement of the goal. It is not about fighting obstacles but about calmly holding your course. The victory here is often mastering your inner contradictions.
reversed: The reversed Chariot may suggest that forces are pulling in opposite directions and it is hard to get moving. Sometimes it is a signal to slow down and check whether the chosen goal is still the right one.
reflection: Where exactly are you heading, and how will you know it is the right way?
Which conflicting needs could you reconcile instead of fighting them?
advice: Go forward. Set a direction, keep to it and do not let yourself be distracted: determination will take you to your goal.
adviceReversed: You are pulling in two directions at once. Decide where you are going before you put your foot down.

name: Strength
symbolism: A woman in a white dress, girded with a garland of flowers, calmly holds a lion's jaws in her hands. Above her head floats the sign of infinity. The animal seems tamed, and the scene is set against gentle hills and a bright yellow sky.
upright: Strength shows a power that has no need for shouting or force. The card encourages you to treat your own emotions and instincts gently, not suppressing them but taming them. This is a courage that comes from patience and kindness towards yourself. Calm is often more persuasive here than pressure.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to doubt in your own strength or to difficulty calming frustration. Then it is worth treating yourself with the patience you show to people you love.
reflection: Which emotion needs understanding today rather than a fight?
Where could your gentleness turn out to be a strength?
advice: Act with gentle strength. Calm, patience and courage will achieve more than pressure. You can handle this.
adviceReversed: You doubt yourself more than you need to. Remind yourself what you have already coped with, and be gentler with yourself.

name: The Hermit
symbolism: An old man in a grey hooded cloak stands on a snowy peak. In one hand he raises a lantern in which a six-pointed star shines; with the other he leans on a long staff. His gaze is turned downwards, as if lighting the way for those who follow him.
upright: The Hermit invites you to stop and look inwards. Time spent in silence can help you separate what is important from what is merely loud. The card does not mean cutting yourself off from people, but consciously making room for your own thoughts. The light of the lantern is enough to see the next step.
reversed: The reversed Hermit may suggest that withdrawal has begun to look like isolation. Sometimes it is the other way round: running from silence because it is hard to face your own questions.
reflection: What do you learn about yourself when you are in silence?
Which one next step can you see in the light you already have?
advice: Step back from the bustle for a while. Think the matter over on your own: the answer will come from within, not from outside.
adviceReversed: The withdrawal has gone on too long. It is time to go out to people and share what you know inside.

name: Wheel of Fortune
symbolism: A great wheel covered with letters and alchemical signs turns in the sky. On its top sits a sphinx with a sword, a serpent slides down one side, and a jackal-headed figure rises from below. In the corners, on clouds, winged creatures (an angel, an eagle, a lion and a bull) bend over books.
upright: The Wheel of Fortune is a reminder that life moves in cycles and no situation stays the same for ever. The card encourages you to notice what is changing right now and to consider how to tune in to it. Not everything depends on us, but our attitude remains in our hands. Change can reveal possibilities that could not be seen before.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to resistance to change, or a feeling that the same pattern keeps coming back. It is an invitation to look for the part of the cycle that can be consciously broken or transformed.
reflection: Which recurring pattern do you notice in your life?
What can you influence even when circumstances change?
advice: The situation is changing, and this is a good moment to go with it. Use the opportunity that appears: the wheel is turning.
adviceReversed: Do not fight what you cannot influence. Focus on what you can do, and wait for the cycle to turn.
